grammar.title: Grammatica
grammar.rule: un libro → il libro; una scatola → la scatola. Il libro è rosso; la scatola è rossa.
grammar.note_en:
Italian uses an article, a small word before a noun, to introduce or identify a thing. A noun names something: libro means “book”, scatola means “box”. Un libro means “a book”; il libro means “the book”, identifying the book already in view or mentioned. Una scatola means “a box”; la scatola means “the box”. Italian nouns have grammatical gender: libro is masculine, scatola feminine. This is a property of the word, not a claim that objects are male or female. Learn the noun with its article. Other article forms come later; these four forms are not a rule for every Italian noun.

An adjective describes a noun. Many adjectives change their ending to agree with its gender: il libro rosso means “the red book”; la scatola rossa means “the red box”. Rosso becomes rossa. Aperto/aperta mean “open”; chiuso/chiusa mean “closed”. Grande means “large” with either gender here; blu likewise keeps the same form. Piccolo/piccola mean “small”. These examples describe one thing: plural forms come next chapter.

È means “is”, with a written accent: la porta è chiusa means “the door is closed”. E without the accent means “and”: Elena e Paolo means “Elena and Paolo”. Ha means “has”: Elena ha la chiave means “Elena has the key”. The h is silent. Non immediately before a verb makes it negative: Elena non apre la busta means “Elena does not open the envelope”. Apre means “opens”; cerca “looks for”; guarda “looks at”; trova “finds”; prende “takes”; mette “puts”. All are forms used here with one named person as subject, the person doing the action. They do not yet show how to say “I open”, “you open”, or “they open”.

Sopra means “on top of/above”; sotto means “under/below”. Dentro means “inside”; fuori means “outside”; qui means “here”. The illustrations and changing positions anchor these words. Dove è la chiave? means “Where is the key?” Chi? means “Who?” For an identified object, la chiave è sotto il libro means “the key is under the book”. To introduce a newly discovered object, this story uses trova: Paolo trova una busta means “Paolo finds an envelope”. An envelope addressed to Ada remains closed: reading its name does not reveal its contents. Scrive means “writes”. Foglio is a sheet of paper, penna a pen, and nome a name. Elena scrive il nome means “Elena writes the name”. The note points Ada to the still-sealed envelope; it does not reveal what the envelope contains. The action table pairs Elena or Paolo with an action: cerca la chiave (“looks for the key”), apre la scatola (“opens the box”), trova la chiave (“finds the key”), prende il libro (“takes the book”), scrive il nome (“writes the name”). The last table pairs un foglio/il foglio (“a sheet/the sheet”), una penna/la penna (“a pen/the pen”) and una busta/la busta (“an envelope/the envelope”).
